In the 1920s and 1930s, Cartland was a prominent young hostess in London society, noted for her beauty, energetic charm and daring parties. Her fashion sense also had a part, and she was one of the first clients of designer [Norman Hartnell](/wiki/Norman_Hartnell "Norman Hartnell"); she remained a client until he died in 1979. He made her presentation and wedding dresses; the latter was made to her own design against Hartnell's wishes, and she admitted it was a failure.

In 1950, Cartland was accused of plagiarism by author [Georgette Heyer](/wiki/Georgette_Heyer "Georgette Heyer"), after a reader drew attention to the apparent borrowing of Heyer's character names, character traits, dialogue and plot points in Cartland's early historical romances. Lee (white) won the fourth game. Lee chose to play a type of extreme strategy, known as *[amashi](/w/index.php?title=Amashi&action=edit&redlink=1 "Amashi (page does not exist)")*, in response to AlphaGo's apparent preference for *[Souba Go](/w/index.php?title=Souba_Go&action=edit&redlink=1 "Souba Go (page does not exist)")* (attempting to win by many small gains when the opportunity arises), taking territory at the perimeter rather than the center.[[57]](#cite_note-ggg4-57) By doing so, his apparent aim was to force an "all or nothing" style of situation – a possible weakness for an opponent strong at negotiation types of play, and one which might make AlphaGo's capability of deciding slim advantages largely irrelevant.[[57]](#cite_note-ggg4-57)

The first 11 moves were identical to the second game, where Lee also played white. In the early game, Lee concentrated on taking territory in the edges and corners of the board, allowing AlphaGo to gain influence in the top and centre. Lee then invaded AlphaGo's region of influence at the top with moves 40 to 48, following the *amashi* strategy. AlphaGo responded with a shoulder hit at move 47, sacrificing four stones elsewhere and gaining the initiative with moves 47 to 53 and 69. Lee tested AlphaGo with moves 72 to 76 without provoking an error, and by this point in the game, commentators had begun to feel Lee's play was a lost cause. However, an unexpected play at white 78, described as "a brilliant *tesuji*", turned the game around.[[57]](#cite_note-ggg4-57) The move developed a white wedge at the centre, and increased the game's complexity.[[58]](#cite_note-Wired_match4-58) [Gu Li](/wiki/Gu_Li_(Go_player) "Gu Li (Go player)") (9p) described it as a "[divine move](/wiki/Divine_move "Divine move")" and stated that the move had been completely unforeseen by him.[[57]](#cite_note-ggg4-57) Move 78 broke new ground as a radical change to playing convention.

The group was formed through the purchase of 51% of [Kia](/wiki/Kia "Kia") by Hyundai Motor Company in 1998. As of 2011, Hyundai owns 33.7%[[4]](#cite_note-4) of Kia Motors.

In June 2021, [Hyundai Motor](/wiki/Hyundai_Motor_Company "Hyundai Motor Company"), [Hyundai Mobis](/wiki/Hyundai_Mobis "Hyundai Mobis"), [Hyundai Glovis](/wiki/Hyundai_Glovis "Hyundai Glovis"), and Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair [Chung Eui-sun](/wiki/Chung_Eui-sun "Chung Eui-sun") collectively purchased an 80% stake in [Boston Dynamics](/wiki/Boston_Dynamics "Boston Dynamics"), which had been under [SoftBank Group](/wiki/SoftBank_Group "SoftBank Group")'s ownership.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

On May 22, 2022, the Hyundai Motor Group announced the company would invest an additional $5 billion in the United States by the year 2025. The investment would strengthen collaboration with US firms in areas such as [urban air mobility](/wiki/Urban_air_mobility "Urban air mobility"), [autonomous driving](/wiki/Autonomous_driving "Autonomous driving"), [artificial intelligence](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence"), and [robotics](/wiki/Robotics "Robotics"). The investments were announced during a visit to South Korea by former President [Joe Biden](/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

On December 10, 2024, Hyundai allowed customers to buy Hyundai cars on [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)"). They could pick it up at their local Hyundai dealership.

Map of the nine colonial colleges

The **colonial colleges** are nine institutions of [higher education](/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") founded in the [Thirteen Colonies](/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies"), predating the [United States](/wiki/United_States "United States"). As the only American universities old enough to have alumni that participated in the [American Revolution](/wiki/American_Revolution "American Revolution") and the [founding of the United States](/wiki/Founding_Fathers_of_the_United_States "Founding Fathers of the United States"), these schools have been identified as a group for their influence on U.S. history.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)

While all nine colonial colleges were founded as [private](/wiki/Private_university "Private university") institutions, two later became [public universities](/wiki/Public_university "Public university"): the [College of William & Mary](/wiki/College_of_William_%26_Mary "College of William & Mary") in 1906, and [Rutgers University](/wiki/Rutgers_University "Rutgers University") in 1945. The remaining seven are all members of the [Ivy League](/wiki/Ivy_League "Ivy League") and remain private to the present day: [Harvard](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), [Yale](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), [Princeton](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University"), [Columbia](/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), [Penn](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), [Brown](/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University"), and [Dartmouth](/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College").
